rationale: Falsified weather or traffic feeds drive unsafe routing across many operations, but injection requires access to or impersonation of a third-party provider.
Leaked strategic and risk documentation enables future targeting and reputational harm but causes no direct flight-safety consequence.
Poisoning the single source of truth propagates corrupted state to every dependent service at once, though write access to the CIS is hard to obtain.
Sensor and IMU injection directly corrupts the control loop and can cause loss of control, but affects aircraft individually rather than the whole volume.
Injected telemetry creates phantom tracks and masks genuine conflicts, and unauthenticated telemetry ingest is readily repeatable once the interface is known.
Log tampering destroys forensic accountability and conceals prior attacks but does not itself endanger flight, and requires privileged SIEM access.
Exploiting regulatory ambiguity lets non-compliant USSPs operate across the whole ecosystem, with systemic but indirect and slow-acting safety erosion.
Weak identity proofing lets an attacker obtain legitimate-looking authorisations, giving accountability loss and unvetted flights rather than immediate loss of control.
A JWT none-algorithm bypass is trivially repeatable, widely documented and yields unrestricted flight authorisation across the service.
Deleting or altering no-fly geometry opens restricted airspace to every operator relying on that database, with severe third-party and infrastructure risk.
GNSS lacks signal authentication, spoofing and jamming hardware is cheap and the effect is immediate loss of positioning over an entire area.
Physical sabotage of vertiport control equipment is locally severe, including during landing, but requires site presence and does not scale.
Injected geofence boundaries cause fleet-wide airspace violations and are trusted implicitly by conformance logic, though feed compromise takes effort.
Backdoored firmware gives full control authority over the airframe, but needs physical or build-chain access and reverse-engineering skill.
Tampering with authority audit records defeats oversight and enforcement across many operators without creating an immediate hazard.
A compromised vendor or substituted component affects every deployed unit, but demands sophisticated, well-resourced and hard-to-detect access.
Loss of ground-station power halts operations and BMS manipulation can cause mid-flight power loss, though effects are bounded to one site or airframe.
Flooding an unprotected gateway is cheap and repeatable and denies authorisation services volume-wide, but is detectable and degrades availability rather than control.
SQL injection yields bulk exfiltration and corruption of flight-plan records using well-known tooling, with mainly confidentiality and integrity consequences.
C2 jamming during BVLOS forces fail-safe or crash, and unauthenticated MAVLink traffic is easy to intercept or manipulate with low-cost SDR.
A leaked API key enables bulk harvesting of sensitive operational data with minimal skill, but confers no control over flights.
